title: Fasting across the church
hook: Orthodox Christians fast most Wednesdays and Fridays; Catholics fast in Lent; many Protestants fast for a cause

segments.voice: Yesterday: fasting, and Jesus saying when you fast, not if, with a washed face. Your line was hunger can pray. What small comfort did you skip? Day one hundred forty-seven.

Three kitchens on the same Friday. In the first, a Greek grandmother is cooking beans and greens in water, no meat, no cheese, no olive oil even, and she's done this most Wednesdays and Fridays of her life. In the second, a Catholic family is having fish sticks, because it's a Friday in Lent. In the third, a young couple from a Baptist church have skipped lunch all week, joining their congregation in praying for a friend with cancer. Three kitchens, three churches, three very different menus. All three would say they're fasting. Today: how the whole church fasts, and how differently.
screen: `A GREEK KITCHEN: BEANS, NO OIL.` → `A CATHOLIC KITCHEN: FISH IN LENT.` → `A BAPTIST COUPLE: NO LUNCH ALL WEEK.`

segments.voice: Fasting across the church. Start at the very beginning. One of the oldest Christian writings outside the Bible, a little handbook called the Didache, probably from the late first or early second century, tells Christians to fast on Wednesdays and Fridays. Many historians connect Friday with the day Jesus died, and Wednesday with the day he was betrayed. That weekly rhythm is still alive. Orthodox Christians keep the strictest fasts. Most Wednesdays and Fridays of the year, plus Great Lent before Easter and several other seasons, they set aside meat, dairy, and often fish, wine and olive oil. Add it up and it can come to half the days of the year. It's done in community, and people are told to adjust for health and circumstance. Catholics keep a lighter, simpler discipline today. On Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, adults fast: one full meal and two small ones. On Fridays in Lent, no meat, which is why the fish sandwich becomes famous every spring. Many Catholics also give up something personal for Lent. Protestant churches vary widely. Anglicans, Lutherans and Methodists often keep Lent. The early Methodists fasted on Fridays, and John Wesley urged it. Many evangelical and Pentecostal churches call a fast for a specific need: a sick friend, a decision, a new year. Some follow the pattern of Daniel, who said: "I ate no pleasant bread, neither came flesh nor wine in my mouth." Different rules, same heart. Each tradition is clearing something away, food, time, a habit, to make space. Space for prayer, for hunger to remind you, and for others. Whether you keep a calendar of fasts or none, the idea underneath is the same: make space.
screen: `THE DIDACHE: WEDNESDAYS AND FRIDAYS.` · `ORTHODOX: THE STRICTEST FASTS.` · `CATHOLICS: FRIDAYS IN LENT.` · `PROTESTANTS: FASTING FOR A CAUSE.` · then, large: `MAKE SPACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Picture this month's calendar. Now pick one day on it. Maybe a Wednesday or a Friday, like the first Christians. Ask what you could fast from that day. It doesn't have to be food. It could be meat, or sugar, or coffee. It could be your phone after dinner, or streaming, or shopping. Choose one. Notice how it feels to decide in advance. If you pray, you can offer that day to God now. If you don't, simply mark it as a day to make space. The bell holds the time.
Fasting across the church. Orthodox, Catholic and Protestant Christians fast by different calendars, all to make space.
Your line: make space. Today, pick one day this month to fast from something, and put it on your calendar. Day one hundred forty-seven.

fork.setup: you're an early Christian reading the Didache. it says to fast twice a week. which days does it choose?
fork.reveal: Wednesdays and Fridays. many historians link them to the betrayal and the crucifixion, and Orthodox Christians still keep them.

trapdoor: what you thought: fasting is one rule everyone follows.
what it means: every church fasts differently, by calendar or by need, all to make space for prayer and for others.
what a scholar hears: Didache 8 sets Wednesday and Friday fasts, apart from the Monday and Thursday fasts of some Jewish groups of the time.

notes: Didache date: commonly given as late 1st or early 2nd century; confirm. Didache 8:1 contrasts its Wednesday/Friday fasts with 'the hypocrites' who fast on Monday and Thursday; the trapdoor phrases this neutrally as 'some Jewish groups of the time' and the voice omits the contrast. Confirm this is handled with care.
Link of Wednesday to the betrayal and Friday to the crucifixion: traditional explanation; stated as 'many historians connect'. Confirm.
Orthodox fast days: 'can come to half the days of the year' (estimates of roughly 180–200). Confirm, and that the pastoral adjustment (economia) is fairly mentioned.

Catholic norms (Latin Church, US): fasting ages 18–59 on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday (one full meal, two smaller meals); abstinence from meat age 14+ on Ash Wednesday and Fridays of Lent. The script simplifies to 'adults' and 'Fridays in Lent'. Confirm.
Early Methodist Friday fasting and Wesley's advocacy: confirm.
Hook scene: Orthodox strict fast often excludes oil; scene is illustrative.
